narrative:
The model determined that you have a 54.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence. Although your decile of 6 was slightly better than the average of accepted students (5.79), the model still interpreted it as increasing your risk of failure. Your LSAT score of 32.5 came next; this was noticeably lower than the 37.2 average among accepted applicants and pushed the prediction more strongly toward failure. Finally, your first-year decile of 4 was well below the accepted-student average of 6 and added further weight toward a negative outcome.

Taken together, these academic performance signals outweighed your upper-middle family income and full-time study plans, both of which are common among accepted students.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic trajectory. Retake the LSAT and aim for a meaningfully higher score, strengthen your study habits to move into a higher class ranking, and consider additional coursework that demonstrates consistent high performance. Once you can show clearer evidence of readiness for the bar exam, reapply. Many students successfully improve these exact areas and gain admission on a later attempt.
